summaryHeading: What a Texas will does that nothing else can
summary: A valid Texas will generally must be in writing, signed by you, and attested by two credible witnesses at least 14 years old (Estates Code Chapter 251). Adding a self-proving affidavit before a notary means the witnesses generally never have to testify in probate.

If you die without a will, the intestacy rules in Estates Code Chapter 201 split your property between your spouse and children by formula — and the split for a blended family or separate property often surprises people.
A will is the document in which you can name a guardian for minor children and direct that their inheritance be held in a testamentary trust until an age you choose.

Our will packages are flat fee, quoted after a free consultation, and typically include the will, a durable power of attorney and medical directives. Bilingual signings available. Book an appointment.

sections.heading: Two Witnesses, a Notary, and the Affidavit Online Forms Skip
paragraphs: The Texas Estates Code keeps the formal requirements short. A will must be in writing, signed by the testator, and attested by at least two credible witnesses at least 14 years old who sign in the testator's presence. A will entirely in your own handwriting — a holographic will — needs no witnesses, but ambiguous homemade wills are where families end up in litigation.

The piece most online forms skip is the self-proving affidavit under the Estates Code. The testator and both witnesses sign a sworn affidavit before a notary at the same time the will is signed. With it, the will can generally be admitted to probate on the affidavit alone. Without it, the executor may have to track down a witness years later and bring them to court — a real problem when the witness was a neighbor who has since moved to Las Cruces or passed away. The wills we draft are signed at our conference table with two staff witnesses and a notary, so the affidavit is done the same day.

sections.heading: Community Property, Separate Property, and the Blended-Family Surprise
paragraphs: Texas calls it intestacy, and Chapter 201 of the Estates Code applies a formula whether you would have liked it or not. The formula turns on a distinction most families never think about: community property (acquired during the marriage) versus separate property (owned before the marriage or received by gift or inheritance).

In general, if all of your children are also your spouse's children, your spouse keeps all of the community property. But if you have a child from a prior relationship — common in El Paso's blended families — your half of the community property goes to all of your children, and your spouse keeps only their own half. The Eastside house you both paid for can end up co-owned by your spouse and your adult child from a first marriage. Separate real property is split differently again: the surviving spouse takes a life estate in one-third of the separate real property, with the remainder of that one-third and the other two-thirds passing to the children (Estates Code §201.002(b)).
With no will, someone has to file a determination of heirship or a small estate affidavit, sometimes with an attorney ad litem to find unknown heirs. A short will skips much of that.

sections.heading: Guardians, Trusts and the Four Will Packages We Draft
paragraphs: For parents, the guardian clause is often the reason to have a will at all. Under the Estates Code a parent may designate in a will who should serve as guardian of their minor children if both parents are gone, and the probate court gives that designation strong weight. Without one, the court chooses among relatives who step forward — and if a grandmother in El Paso and an uncle in Phoenix both apply, the family fights it out.

The second issue is money. A minor cannot manage inherited property outright, so without planning the court may have to appoint a guardian of the estate and supervise it until the child turns 18 — then hand over everything at once. A testamentary trust inside the will avoids that. You name a trustee, say what the money can be used for, and pick the age at which the child receives the balance — 21, 25, or in stages. The trust only comes into existence if it is needed.

sections.heading: Divorce, Marriage, a New Baby: When the Old Will Stops Fitting
paragraphs: A will is not a one-time document. In general, divorce revokes gifts to and appointments of a former spouse under the Estates Code, but it does not rewrite the rest of the will or touch beneficiary designations on life insurance and retirement accounts, which pass outside the will. Marriage after a will is signed does not by itself revoke it in Texas, so a will leaving everything to your parents can stay in force after you marry. A child born or adopted after the will may be entitled to a share as a pretermitted child, but the result is messy and rarely what you intended.

Other triggers: buying a house, a child turning 18, a named executor or guardian moving away or passing, and a move out of Texas. Updates are usually a new will rather than a codicil; if we drafted the original, an update is a reduced fee. While you are at it, update the companion documents — a medical power of attorney naming a former spouse can stay effective until revoked.

faqs.q: Does a will in Texas need to be notarized?
faqs.a: No — a will needs two witnesses, not a notary. But the self-proving affidavit that accompanies it does require a notary, and that is what generally lets the will be probated without calling the witnesses. We include it in every will we draft.

faqs.q: Is an online or handwritten will valid in Texas?
faqs.a: It can be. A holographic will in your own handwriting needs no witnesses, and a typed form will is valid if properly witnessed. The problems come later: ambiguous wording, no self-proving affidavit and no plan for minor children can cost the family more in probate than a drafted will costs now.

faqs.q: What happens to our house if my spouse dies without a will?
faqs.a: In general, if the house is community property and all of your spouse's children are also yours, you keep it. If your spouse had a child from another relationship, that child inherits a share of your spouse's half and you become co-owners. A will avoids that.

faqs.q: Can I name a guardian for my children in my will?
faqs.a: Yes, and the court gives a parent's written designation strong weight. We also recommend naming an alternate and pairing it with a testamentary trust so the inheritance is managed until an age you choose.

faqs.q: Do you do wills in Spanish?
faqs.a: We conduct the consultation and the signing in Spanish and can provide a Spanish translation for your records. The will that is probated is in English.
